procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated May 3, 1968 of the Patna High Court in Criminal W.J.C. No. 17 of 1968 and Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 447 of 1968.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed a Writ Petition and an application under s. 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure in the Patna High Court, seeking a writ of habeas corpus and an order of a like nature. Both were heard together and dismissed by a common judgment on May 3, 1968.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the Patna High Court's dismissal of his Writ Petition and application under s. 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant's detention was illegal because he was not produced before a magistrate within 24 hours of his arrest.

facts: The appellant claimed he was arrested on February 18, 1968, but was not produced before a magistrate within the required 24-hour period.
The court was presented with the order-sheet from the Laheriasarai Police Station case.
law: Section 167 of the Code of Criminal Procedure requires an arrested person to be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours of their arrest.
application: The court examined the police station's order-sheet.
This official record showed that the appellant was, in fact, produced before the Magistrate on February 18, 1968.
reasoning.conclusion: The court rejected the appellant's claim because the official order-sheet directly contradicted his allegation, proving that he had been produced before a magistrate within 24 hours of his arrest.

issue.issue_text: Whether the magistrate's order-sheet, which recorded the appellant's production on several days, had been falsely made, thereby invalidating the detention.

facts: The Supreme Court acknowledged the High Court's finding that the magistrate had wrongly recorded in the order-sheet that the appellant was produced in court on several occasions when remand orders were made.
A report from the jail superintendent confirmed that the appellant was not produced on those dates because he himself had refused to leave the jail.
law: Remand orders can be lawfully passed in the absence of an accused person if, for some reason, they cannot be brought before the magistrate.
application: The Court distinguished between the incorrect entries about the appellant's physical presence and the validity of the remand orders themselves.
It reasoned that the wrong entries did not mean that the remand orders were not, in fact, passed by the magistrate.
The Court noted that the appellant's absence was due to his own refusal to appear, and therefore he could not legitimately complain that the orders were passed in his absence.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument. It held that even though the order-sheet contained false entries regarding the appellant's production, the underlying remand orders were still validly passed. Since the orders could be lawfully made in the appellant's self-imposed absence, the detention was not invalidated.

issue.issue_text: Whether a magistrate has the power to detain an accused in jail for a period exceeding 15 days in total.

facts: The appellant argued that the magistrate had no power to detain him in jail for a total period exceeding 15 days.
The magistrate had passed multiple remand orders, each for a period of up to 15 days, extending the appellant's detention beyond the initial 15-day period.
law: The Supreme Court distinguished between two sections of the Code of Criminal Procedure: Section 167 and Section 344.
Section 167 applies during the initial investigation stage, immediately after arrest. Under this section, a magistrate can order custody for a maximum period of 15 days 'in the whole'.
Section 344 applies during the later stage of inquiries and trials. Under this section, a magistrate can remand an accused to jail custody for a term 'not exceeding 15 days at a time'.
application: The Court determined that the appellant's argument that detention was limited to 15 days in total was based on Section 167.
However, the Court found that the proceedings had progressed to a stage where Section 344 was applicable.
Under Section 344, the magistrate was competent to pass remand orders from time to time, as long as each individual order was for a period not exceeding 15 days.

The Court noted that the conditions for applying Section 344 had been met, specifically that sufficient evidence had been collected to raise a suspicion that the accused may have committed an offence.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument. It held that the 15-day total limit on detention applies only under Section 167 during the initial investigation. Once the case moves to the inquiry or trial stage, Section 344 empowers the magistrate to remand the accused for successive periods, each not exceeding 15 days at a time.

issue.issue_text: Whether the conditions for passing remand orders in excess of 15 days were satisfied.

facts: The appellant argued that the Magistrate had no power to detain him in jail for more than 15 days in total, contending that the proceedings were governed by s. 167 of the Code.

The prosecution's case before the Magistrate was that the appellant had confessed to the police, and two other individuals had also made confessions that implicated the appellant in dacoity offenses (under s. 395 of the Code).
law: The Court determined that the power to remand was governed by s. 344 of the Code, not s. 167.
The Court clarified that s. 344 can be applied even before a charge-sheet is submitted, while an investigation is still ongoing.
Under s. 344, a Magistrate can pass remand orders from time to time, each for a period not exceeding 15 days, provided a specific condition is met.

The condition is that sufficient evidence must have been collected to raise a suspicion that the accused may have committed an offense, and it appears likely that further evidence may be obtained by granting the remand.
application: The Court found that the Magistrate had satisfied the condition required by s. 344.

The evidence presented to the Magistrate, specifically the appellant's own confession and two other confessions implicating him, was deemed sufficient to raise a suspicion that he had committed an offense and that further evidence might be obtained.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that since the conditions of s. 344 were satisfied, the Magistrate was competent to pass remand orders from time to time, each not exceeding 15 days, thus allowing for a total detention period beyond 15 days. Consequently, the Court rejected the appellant's argument that the conditions for such remand orders were not met.

issue.issue_text: Whether any remand orders were factually passed by the magistrate.

facts: The magistrate's order sheet contained entries incorrectly stating that the appellant was produced before him when subsequent remand orders were made.
The High Court found these entries to be wrong, as a report from the jail superintendent showed the appellant had refused to leave the jail on those dates.
On March 28, 1968, the appellant was represented by counsel before the magistrate.
At that time, the appellant's counsel did not argue that no remand orders had ever been passed. Instead, counsel argued about which section of the law governed the remand (s. 167 vs. s. 344).
law: A magistrate's incorrect recording of an accused person's presence does not mean that a remand order was not actually passed in their absence.
Remand orders can be lawfully passed in the absence of an accused if they cannot be brought before the magistrate for some reason.
application: The Supreme Court agreed with the High Court that the magistrate had wrongly recorded the appellant's presence.
However, the Court reasoned that these "wrong entries" did not mean that "the remand orders were not in fact passed by him."

The Court found it significant that the appellant's own counsel, on March 28, argued about the legality of the remand orders rather than their existence, which implicitly acknowledged that the orders had been passed.
The Court also noted that the contention that no orders were passed at all did not appear to have been raised in the High Court.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, concluding that it was "not possible to say that remand orders were not passed." The Court held that while the magistrate's record of the appellant's presence was incorrect, the remand orders themselves were factually made, albeit in the appellant's absence.

issue.issue_text: Whether remand orders passed in the absence of the accused are lawful.

facts: The jail superintendent's report confirmed that on several occasions, the appellant (the accused) was not produced before the magistrate when remand orders were passed.
The reason for his non-production was that the appellant himself had refused to leave the jail to appear before the magistrate.
The magistrate had incorrectly recorded in the order sheet that the appellant was present on these occasions.
law: Remand orders can be lawfully and validly passed in the absence of an accused person if, for some reason, their presence cannot be secured.
application: The Court applied this legal principle to the facts, noting that the appellant's presence could not be secured specifically because he refused to appear.
Because the appellant's absence was his own fault, the Court reasoned that he could not legitimately make a grievance that the orders were passed in his absence.

The Court also determined that the magistrate's error of wrongly recording the appellant's presence did not invalidate the underlying remand orders, which were otherwise lawfully passed under the circumstances.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the remand orders were lawful. It held that such orders can be validly passed in the absence of the accused if their presence cannot be secured. In this case, since the accused himself refused to be produced in court, he could not complain about orders being passed in his absence, and his detention was therefore valid.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant's detention was invalid because he was never informed of the grounds for his arrest.

facts: The appellant contended that his detention was invalid because he was never informed of the grounds for his arrest.
The appellant's own case was that the police had tortured him and threatened to involve him in dacoity cases unless he made certain incriminating statements.
In an application made from jail, the appellant alleged that a police officer asked him to 'admit that offence'.
The appellant was aware that an identification parade was going to be held and refused to participate.
law: Article 22(1) of the Constitution requires that a person who is arrested be informed of the grounds for such arrest.
application: The Court found the appellant's allegation to be 'without any foundation'.
The Court reasoned that the appellant must have realized the grounds for his arrest from the fact that the police were trying to get him to make incriminating statements related to dacoity cases.
The appellant's own application, in which he mentioned being asked to 'admit that offence', indicated he was aware of the charge against him.
The Court also pointed to the appellant's knowledge of the upcoming identification parade as further evidence that he was not ignorant of the reasons for his arrest.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the facts of the case contradicted ('negative the suggestion') the appellant's claim of being kept in ignorance of the reasons for his arrest, and therefore rejected this contention.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant's detention was illegal due to the absence of a valid custody warrant.

facts: The appellant argued that his detention in jail was illegal because the jail authorities did not have a valid custody warrant.
He pointed to a warrant dated February 18, 1968, which he claimed was cancelled because a magistrate's note on it indicated he was remanded to police custody instead.
On February 21, 1968, the magistrate ordered the appellant to be taken into jail custody.
law: The court operates on a presumption of regularity, meaning it assumes that judicial and official acts (like a magistrate issuing a warrant or a jail superintendent accepting a prisoner) are performed correctly unless there is evidence to the contrary.
application: The Court first assumed, for the sake of argument, that the February 18 warrant was indeed cancelled.
However, it found no evidence to prove that a fresh custody warrant was not issued on February 21, when the order for jail custody was made.
The Court reasoned that the magistrate would have known that the jail authorities would not accept a prisoner without a proper custody warrant.
Therefore, the Court concluded there was no reason to believe that the magistrate failed to issue the necessary warrant or that the jail superintendent would have accepted the appellant without one.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's contention, finding it to be "wholly without any basis." It concluded that it was reasonable to presume a valid custody warrant had been issued on February 21, 1968, in accordance with standard procedure.

cases.principle: The power under s. 344 of the Code of Criminal Procedure can be exercised even before the submission of the charge-sheet, at the stage when the investigation is still not over.
The power under s. 344 of the Code of Criminal Procedure can be exercised even before the submission of the charge-sheet, at the stage when the investigation is still not over.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A Magistrate's power under Section 344 to remand an accused to custody can be exercised even before the submission of a charge-sheet, while the investigation is still ongoing. The placement of Section 344 in the chapter on inquiries and trials does not restrict its application to only those stages. Under this section, a Magistrate is competent to pass remand orders from time to time, with each order not exceeding 15 days, provided the conditions in the Explanation to the section are satisfied.
obiter: Assuming a custody warrant was cancelled, there is nothing to show that a fresh custody warrant had not been issued when the Magistrate ordered the appellant to be taken into jail custody.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: In our view none of the contentions raised on behalf of the appellant can be sustained. The appeal, therefore, fails and has to be rejected. The court found that the appellant's detention was lawful as it was governed by Section 344 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which permits repeated remands to jail custody, and that the procedural and factual challenges raised by the appellant were either procedurally flawed or factually unsubstantiated.
legal_tests_applied: The court distinguished between Section 167 and Section 344 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Section 167 applies at the initial investigation stage, allowing for a maximum total detention of 15 days in either police or jail custody. Section 344 applies once an inquiry or trial has begun, permitting a magistrate to remand an accused to jail custody for a term not exceeding 15 days at a time, provided sufficient evidence has been collected to raise a suspicion of an offense and it seems likely that further evidence may be obtained.
why_appellant_lost: The argument that the magistrate's order-sheet was falsely made was rejected because, while the court acknowledged the entries regarding the appellant's presence were incorrect, this did not invalidate the fact that the remand orders themselves were passed.

The contention that a magistrate cannot detain an accused for more than 15 days in total was dismissed. The court determined the proceedings were at the 'inquiry' stage, making Section 344 of the Code applicable, which allows for repeated remands of up to 15 days at a time, as opposed to the 15-day total limit under Section 167.

The claim that the appellant was never informed of the grounds for his arrest failed on a procedural basis, as the court noted that his writ petition 'did not charge that at the time of his arrest he was not informed of the grounds for his arrest.'

The argument that the detention was illegal due to the absence of a valid custody warrant was rejected as 'wholly without any basis.' The court reasoned inferentially that 'jail authorities would not accept the appellant in jail unless the police taking him there produced a custody warrant' and there was 'no reason to think' that the magistrate had not issued one.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position that Section 344 of the Code of Criminal Procedure governed the detention was upheld. The court agreed that since an inquiry had begun, the magistrate was competent 'to pass remand orders from time to time so long as each of those orders was not for a period in excess of 15 days.'

The respondent successfully argued that even if the magistrate's record of the appellant's presence was incorrect, it did not mean the remand orders were not factually passed, a conclusion the court accepted.

The respondent prevailed on the issue of the custody warrant because the court found the appellant's claim to be unsubstantiated and inferred the existence and validity of the warrant from the standard procedure of jail intake.
The respondent succeeded in defeating the claim regarding the grounds for arrest by pointing out that the appellant had failed to properly raise this specific issue in his writ petition.
policy_considerations: The court articulated the legislative policy behind Section 167, stating its object is twofold: 'one that the law does not favour detention in police custody except in special cases... and secondly, to enable such a person to make a representation before a magistrate.'

The court explained the policy behind the custody provisions in Section 344, noting that it provides for jail custody only, 'the object being that once an inquiry or a trial begins it is not proper to let the accused remain under police influence.'
